# 17-expanse — sources

Back-test entry `17-expanse.yaml`: Expanse, job sizes predicted at submit time on shared GPU clusters (YC Spring 2026,
P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era
where one exists; anything later is marked as later and sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Expanse - Unlock wasted GPU capacity", 2026-05-04 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/QCF-expanse-unlock-wasted-gpu-capacity

- [YCP] YC company page, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/expanse
- [SITE] expanse.sh, read 2026-10-22 — https://expanse.sh

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

- Rafael Moreno → author's invention: a vague, habitual story (GUESSED), echoing [HN] "everyone over-requests by two to three times".
- Ingrid Haugen → author's invention: a gate No (writing up, no jobs that week).
- Samuel Adeyemi → author's invention: a gate No (away at a conference).
- Yusuf Demir → [HN] "snooping on sumbit scripts ... many of them are egregiously bad": a copied script holding eight GPUs.
- Claire Dubois-Martin → author's invention, filling a gap: a licensed binary with no source code, so the tested condition fails ('no').
- Hiroshi Takeda → [HN] "at least for everyone else, I'd would prefer tuning my own usage myself": he profiles a test run (Current solution mostly works; Adoption friction no).
- Fatima Al-Sayed → [HN] "you lose days of work"; the walltime limit and the group allocation are the author's.
- Diego Castañeda → [HN] the student's PDE simulation ("If I'm running a PDE simulation, and I allocate n machines I want to use all of them"); he keeps his margin (Adoption friction probably not).

Cluster operators (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.
- Arjun Mehta → [HN] "large scale compute industries as well, such as quant funds": a quant-fund platform lead who owns the compute budget, sees more waste than the founder's high and decides alone (against the tested department head).
- Beatrix Okoro → [HN] "What you are really left with is the 'small and medium business' clusters that are purpose specific": a small cluster, less waste, a lower rung.
- Thomas Reinholt → [HN] the security objection ("a hard no"); would not pay.
- Leilani Kahale → [HN] "In many places the cost of the HPC hardware isn't passed onto them": a grant-funded university cluster that does not measure the waste (dont_know) and has no line for a monthly fee.

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem to solution to sending, but the look-back window (screen 4) sits between two halves of the same context screen (3 and 5), when it would read better after the context is defined.

screens.why4: The source-code and Python rows are real conditions, but 'went through SLURM or Kubernetes as usual' is already true of my whole segment, so it takes a slot that a live condition should have.
screens.why5: The rows keep my meaning, but the belief drifts: the clause keeps its own subject and gets pasted after 'For most researchers' and 'Most researchers', which mangles what I meant.
screens.why7: The picked row is healthy, since it is true for some researchers and false for others, such as anyone running a licensed binary, but several shape rules bend: the rows are not subjectless verb phrases, so the belief reads broken; the SLURM/Kubernetes row is one the segment already settles; and no row is marked as suggested with a reason.
screens.instead: Which of these is most likely to be missing? · kept the job's source code on the cluster beside the submit script (suggested: a licensed binary or code kept elsewhere leaves the model nothing to read) · wrote the job's code in Python · Keel will test: Most researchers who run jobs on shared GPU clusters kept the job's source code on the cluster beside the submit script; holds if no more than 1 in 3 say No.

screens.why1: Right after compatibility, asking what Expanse does better than padding requests by hand is the obvious next question before the switch is tested.
screens.why2: Plain to me: 'better than the way they do it today' and 'benefits that would make them switch' is how I'd talk about getting researchers off their 2-3x over-requesting habit.
screens.why3: I know what my product changes for a researcher at submit time (no OOM mid-run, no resubmits, smaller requests fit sooner), so I can answer from my own material.
screens.why4: The only chip is the escape, 'Leave this out of the study', which fits a founder who can't name a benefit; the box takes my own words.
screens.why5: Both my benefits are kept in order, but my first one went in verbatim as a clause, so the belief reads 'given them the job runs first time', which is broken English though the meaning is still mine.
screens.why7: Both benefits are carried in order and joined with 'and', and the escape is present, but one rule is bent: the first row is a clause, not the noun phrase the card requires, so the belief is ungrammatical; the hint's 25 words also sits loose against the card's 9 words a row.
screens.instead: What does it do better than the way they do it today? Hint: one benefit a line, a few words each (e.g. 'a job that runs first time, no resubmits'); belief: 'For most, with it, their last job submission would have given them a job that runs first time, with no resubmits, and a shorter wait in the queue.'

screens.why1: Checking the benefits Keel drafted right after I typed what it does better is the obvious next step before the belief is fixed.
screens.why2: The rows are in my words, but the belief reads ungrammatically ('would have given them the job runs first time, no resubmits'), so I had to read it twice.
screens.why3: Jobs running first time without resubmits and shorter queue waits for right-sized requests are exactly what my researchers live with at every submission.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and mine, but the first is a clause with a comma tail rather than a noun phrase, which is what breaks the belief sentence.
screens.why5: Both my benefits are kept as rows, but the Keel-will-test box drops the shorter queue wait, and the intro says strangers will 'tick from' my benefits, which is not what I agreed to.
screens.why7: The stranger's fixed four with 'I can't tell' keep the balance, but the test box keeps only the first benefit while the belief carries both (the card's named pitfall), and the first row is not the noun phrase the shape asks for.
screens.instead: Rows: 'Jobs that run first time, with no resubmits' · 'A shorter wait in the queue'; test box: 'For most, with it, their last job submission would have given them jobs that run first time, with no resubmits and a shorter wait in the queue'; intro: 'Strangers will be asked whether it would have done their last submission better, a lot, a little, no difference or worse.'

screens.why1: Right after what it does better, asking what my researchers must do to start using it is the obvious next question about the solution.
screens.why2: Setup, extra steps and learning are plain words to me, and padding and line-level fixes are how my researchers talk about job requests.
screens.why3: I know exactly what we ask of a researcher: take our predicted sizes instead of their 2-3x margin, and apply the code fixes we flag.
screens.why4: The only option is the escape chip, and 'Leave this out of the study' fits a founder who has nothing to say here.
screens.why5: The belief, 'Most would use the suggested sizes instead of padding', is my first effort word for word, and the frame keeps it as part of the solution.
screens.why7: Both efforts are steps the researcher takes themselves. Each is a base-form phrase under 9 words in one voice, neither repeats what Compatibility or Purchase friction tests, and the belief is on the would-they-take-this-effort measure with the founder's escape present.

screens.why1: Right after I typed what researchers have to do to start, Keel shows the efforts back for me to check, which is the obvious next step before picking one to test.
screens.why2: 'Suggested sizes', 'padding' and 'line-level code fixes' are how my researchers and I talk about jobs and requests; the only blemish is the intro repeating the title word for word.
screens.why3: Both rows are things a researcher at a SLURM or K8s cluster does with their own hands at submit time, trusting the predicted request and editing their own script.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts, one per row, my own words, no bundling, and neither repeats what Compatibility (source on the cluster, Python) or Purchase friction (security review) already test.
screens.why5: These are the two adoption steps from my own material, using the suggested sizes rather than padding and applying the code fixes, kept as I would say them.
screens.why7: Each row is one effort the researcher takes themselves, a base-form verb phrase within 9 words, 2 of the 1 to 4 allowed, and the belief 'Most would use the suggested sizes instead of padding' can plainly be supported or refuted by Yes / Only if / Probably not / No; the intro's 'under 9 words' is a hair stricter than the card's 'at most 9' but bends nothing in the rows.
screens.instead: Keep the two rows; reword the intro to 'Reword, remove or add; at most 9 words each. You pick the one to test next.' so it doesn't repeat the title or undercount the limit.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the efforts Keel wrote from my answer, picking the one to test is the obvious next step before the stranger's item is built.
screens.why2: Padding a request and line-level code fixes are how I and the researchers on our clusters talk, so both rows read first time.
screens.why3: I know which step is the real hurdle from the HN thread: people trust their own margin more than a model's number, so I can pick from what I know.
screens.why4: Both are my own efforts, distinct, in my words, and either is a sensible pick; no row is padding or a duplicate.
screens.why5: The rows and the belief are word for word what I typed, and 'nothing is reworded here' holds.
screens.why7: Both rows are steps the researcher takes themselves, on the one measure of extra effort to start using it, base-form and in one voice, with nothing Compatibility or Purchase friction already tests; the picked belief can be supported by Yes or Only if and refuted by Probably not or No, and the item will carry I can't tell.

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out is the obvious point to decide whether strangers get a sign-up line at the end, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: Pilot is my own word, since I sell a two-week measurement and then a paid pilot, and the hint says exactly what respondents will see.
screens.why3: I know I want leads, but the screen doesn't say whether the line goes to researchers or to cluster operators, and a researcher can't put an agent on every node of the cluster, so I'm half guessing whose emails I'd get.
screens.why4: Yes or no is the whole choice here, the two options are distinct, and no escape is needed for a decision the founder makes.
screens.why5: My Yes is kept, and 'Would you try this for real?' doesn't misstate my offer, though it is lighter than my free measurement followed by a paid pilot.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? Cluster operators who say yes get a line at the end: "Want a free two-week waste measurement on your cluster? Leave your email." (Yes, ask operators / Yes, ask everyone / No pilot)

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs here, just before the study goes out to researchers, and it is clear why it is asked.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint packs in video, on-screen text, a one-time voice recording, 400 credits and text messages, so I need a second read; it also says 'voice' while the video and my pick talk about a face.
screens.why3: Picking the interviewer is my own call as the founder, and I can decide it by listening to two five-second samples.
screens.why4: Two distinct voices, each with a sample to hear and one preselected, is complete for this choice, and no escape chip is needed.
screens.why5: The screen does not touch my problem, solution or roles; it only sets who delivers the questions, so nothing I typed has drifted.
screens.instead: Who should ask researchers your questions on the video? Daphne (picked) / Saskia, tap to hear each. Hint: one choice per project, 400 credits either way; the link goes out by text message.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the researchers, deciding how they answer is the obvious next step before sending.
screens.why2: Plain words; 'AI interviewer', 'read and tap' and 'link' are clear to me and to an ML founder.
screens.why3: It is my call about my own study and I know researchers would rather read and tap between jobs than sit through a video.
screens.why4: Three distinct, complete choices covering voice, text and both, with no escape needed on a format pick.
screens.why5: My pick 'Read and tap' is kept and the screen says 'researchers', my own word.

screens.why1: Right after choosing how researchers answer, the last step is who receives the links, so it is obvious why it is asked here at the end of the flow.
screens.why2: Each option reads plainly on first pass, and the one Keel-specific term ('the Contacts page') is explained in its own line.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I would send this to: researchers I have met at HPC centres and labs, by name, so this is answerable from my own situation.
screens.why4: The three routes (people I name, a Keel list, one open link posted where they gather, such as a cluster users' list or Slack) are distinct and cover how I would reach researchers; no option is missing or doubled.
screens.why5: My pick, people I know by name each with their own link, is shown back as I chose it, with nothing changed.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits under the title and on every card, with the deciding number beside it (4 counted, 5 needed to call it), so I know why there is no answer yet; the headline names only Compatibility although all three cards are stuck the same way.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart on the stage page, but the tally (3 beliefs, 3 too few to call), the count (7 answered, 4 counted) and the bar (5 needed) are plain; why 3 of my 7 researchers were not counted is nowhere on the screen, so I have to go looking.
screens.why_b3: The three belief lines are the ones I checked, though Relative advantage still shows the queue-wait clause Keel said it would drop; the solution statement under the title is garbled ('the researcher installed on every node and hooked into SLURM') and does not read as my product.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I need at least one more counted answer per belief, but the screen never says so, and it doesn't say whether to send the study to more researchers or why three answers were not counted.

screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it does not say that one more counted answer would call it, or that 3 of 4 already lean my way.

screens.why1: As the first screen it is obvious why it is asked: it checks I run jobs on the kind of cluster the study is about before anything else.
screens.why2: SLURM, Kubernetes and GPUs are my everyday words, though 'work on' is a little loose next to the 'submit jobs to' I would say.
screens.why3: I know which cluster I submit to and roughly how big it is, though someone on a cluster near the 100 line might have to think about it.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it for a screener, and a gate needs no escape.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product or the founder's plan reaches me, only the cluster I already use.
screens.why6: Said aloud, 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' is clunky for a yes-or-no question where the guidelines give the screener as the stem then 'Yes or no.'
screens.instead: Do you submit jobs to a SLURM or Kubernetes cluster with 100 or more GPUs? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I'm on a 100-plus GPU cluster, asking whether a job of mine actually died over its resource request this week is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: I'd say a job 'got killed' or 'OOM'd' rather than 'lost a job to a wrong resource request', and 'lose a job' heard aloud half-sounds like losing your actual job, so it takes a beat.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether any of my runs got killed for under-requesting memory or hitting the time limit in the last week.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it cleanly, and the chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not this gate.
screens.why5: Nothing about anyone's product or plan comes through; it's just about my jobs.
screens.why6: One short question with 'Yes or no' is easy to answer after hearing it once.
screens.why7: The stem asks the costly thing, a job lost to a bad request, not the circumstance of guessing resources, so a researcher whose jobs all ran can truly say No and one who got killed says Yes, on two fixed answers with no escape.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did any of your jobs get killed because you asked for too little memory, GPUs or time? Yes or No.

screens.why1: Right after I said whether I lost a job to a bad resource request, showing me a tool that predicts those requests is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: SLURM, Kubernetes, walltime, GPU memory, submission script: these are the words I use every day, so I get it on one read.
screens.why3: Guessing memory, GPUs and walltime at submit is exactly what I do, so I can judge this from my own runs.
screens.why4: A card to read with no options.
screens.why5: It is the idea card shown on purpose, described in plain cluster terms, and nothing reads like the founder's internal jargon about me.
screens.why6: Heard once, the middle runs long: five clipped sentences, a run of 'GPU memory, memory, CPUs and walltime', and 'Failed jobs get why and how to fix it' trips the ear.
screens.instead: Imagine Expanse, a cluster tool that predicts job resources. At submit it reads your code and script and predicts GPU memory, CPUs and walltime, and when a job fails it tells you why and how to fix it. The people building it believe it would let you get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.

screens.why1: Right after the Expanse card a question about where my code sits is abrupt; I can't see why it matters to a tool that predicts resources.
screens.why2: The stem has no subject ('Had your source code sitting...'), so I have to read it twice to know it means 'Was my code on the cluster?'.
screens.why3: I know where my code was when I last submitted a job.
screens.why4: 'Yes, with some steps' makes no sense for whether my code was on the cluster; it either was or it wasn't, though the escape fits.
screens.why5: It drifts into the tool's own plumbing, needing my code on the cluster, rather than asking about how I set my requests.
screens.why6: Heard aloud, the fragment 'Had your source code sitting on the cluster?' sounds broken, though the three options and the escape say fine.
screens.why7: Everyone in this segment runs jobs from code on a SLURM or Kubernetes cluster, so every answer is Yes and nothing can count against; the condition the pitch rests on, letting a prediction set my memory, GPUs and time, is never tested.
screens.instead: Think of your last job submission. Could you have let a tool set its memory, GPUs and run time for you? Yes, easily · Yes, most of the time · Only sometimes · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the question about my code sitting on the cluster, it's obvious they want to know whether this tool would have helped my last submission.
screens.why2: Job submission, cluster and the four options are all words I use every day, and I can answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: I remember my last submission and what I guessed for memory, GPUs and walltime, so I can judge whether a predictor would have changed it.
screens.why4: The four answers are distinct and cover the range from a lot better to worse, and I can't tell is the right escape for a hypothetical.
screens.why5: Only the idea card's own line reaches me, shown on purpose, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms leaks into the question.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, with four short options and one escape, easy to hold when heard once.
screens.why7: The measure, the fixed four, the two-for and two-against balance and the I can't tell escape all meet the card, but the stem bends a rule: 'go better' leaves which better unclear, and 'my last job submission' is any last one, maybe one that ran fine, rather than one where my resource guess was at stake.
screens.instead: Think of the last job you had to guess memory, GPUs and run time for. Would Expanse have got that request right better, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: After asking whether Expanse would have helped my last submission, asking whether I'd actually trust its sizes over my own padding is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: Padding a request is exactly what I do and call it, and suggested sizes for a job are plain to me on first hearing.
screens.why3: Whether I'd drop my padding is my own call on every submission, so I can answer it from what I do.
screens.why4: The four are distinct and the escape fits, but the fixed 'Yes, if it was clearly worth it' hides my real catch, which is that I'd only trust it if an under-sized guess didn't kill a multi-day run.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks beyond the idea card shown on purpose; 'suggested sizes' and 'padding' are my words, not a founder's product terms.
screens.why6: Heard once it is short, one question, four short options and one escape said last.
screens.why7: The effort is mine to take, on the one measure, with two options for and two against and the I can't tell escape, but the conditional is the plain fallback rather than an Only if naming what the step risks in my work, the pitfall the card names.
screens.instead: To use Expanse, you'd use its suggested sizes instead of your usual padding. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Only if a job it sized never died mid-run · Probably not · No · I can't tell
